Where it began

Bishan Singh Bedi was born in Amritsar, then part of British India, on 25 September 1946. He came to cricket late, yet only two years after taking it up he was bowling for Northern Punjab, aged just fifteen.

He moved to Delhi in 1968–69. In the 1974–75 Ranji Trophy he took 64 wickets, a record, and that same season he returned figures of 7 for 5 against Jammu and Kashmir. He also spent many summers in England with Northamptonshire. By the end he had 1,560 first-class wickets, more than any other Indian bowler had managed.

The player

Bedi played 67 Tests for India between 1966 and 1979 and took 266 wickets at 28.71. He had 14 five-wicket innings and one ten-wicket match, and his best figures, 7 for 98, came at Calcutta against Australia in 1969–70. He was one quarter of India's famous spin quartet, and some of his series were outstanding: 22 wickets at 13.18 against New Zealand in 1976–77, and 31 in Australia the following season, including 10 for 194 in the match at Perth.

He took over the captaincy from Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi in 1976 and led India in 22 Tests. His first win in charge came at Port of Spain, where India made 406 in the fourth innings, a record at the time. A 2–0 home series win over New Zealand followed.

What made him special

People who watched him used words like graceful and beautiful. He was a master of flight, and he could make the ball dip early or drift on and add small changes of spin. His action was so easy and smooth that he could bowl for hours without losing his line, a gift to any captain. In 2008 Wisden listed him among the five best cricketers never chosen as one of its Cricketers of the Year.

His batting was another story. He made 656 Test runs at 8.99, and his one Test fifty, 50 not out against New Zealand at Kanpur in 1976, must have surprised everyone, him included. Yet he once won a Gillette Cup semi-final for Northamptonshire against Hampshire by hitting a boundary off the second-last ball.

Away from the middle

On the field he was easy to spot in his colourful patka. He received the Padma Shri in 1970 and the Arjuna Award, and in 2004 the Indian board gave the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award to all four members of the spin quartet together, Bedi alongside Bhagwat Chandrasekhar, Srinivas Venkatraghavan and Erapalli Prasanna.

He once explained that doing his own washing, all his life, was fine exercise for a spinner's shoulders and fingers. He died in 2023, aged 77.

And finally

At the 1975 World Cup, against East Africa at Headingley, he bowled his full 12 overs. Eight were maidens, and the other four cost six runs between them. He took a wicket too, almost as an afterthought. It is a lovely reminder that a slow bowler could be every bit as hard to score off as a fast one.
